short: ISO/IEC 27090:2026, published 14 October 2026, is ISO and IEC guidance on detecting and mitigating security threats specific to AI systems, such as data poisoning and model theft. It is guidance, not a certifiable standard.
title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026, AI Security Threats
subtitle: Guidance on security threats and compromises to AI systems
body_html:
On this page

  • What ISO/IEC 27090 is
  • What it is not: a certificate
  • How it got here: the ISO life cycle
  • How it relates to the other frameworks
  • How to put ISO 27090 to work: a 5-step path
  • Frequently asked questions about ISO/IEC 27090
  • What independent commentary says
  • How this page was written
  • Primary sources on ISO/IEC 27090

The one-paragraph answer

ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is international guidance on security threats and compromises specific to AI systems, published on 14 October 2026 by ISO and IEC (edition 1, 56 pages, CHF 204). It comes from ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27, the committee that maintains ISO/IEC 27001. ISO describes it as guidance on understanding, detecting and mitigating AI-specific threats across the AI life cycle, such as data poisoning and model theft. It is guidance, not a certifiable requirements standard, so no organisation can be certified to it. It is meant to sit beside ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, not replace them.

What ISO/IEC 27090 is

The full title is ISO/IEC 27090:2026, Cybersecurity, Artificial intelligence (AI), Addressing security threats and compromises to AI systems. It is a joint publication of the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission, developed in subcommittee SC 27 of their joint technical committee JTC 1, which is responsible for information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection and maintains the ISO/IEC 27000 family. ISO files it under ICS 35.030, IT security.

ISO's public description of the scope, as our editor checked it on 18 October 2026, is short: understanding, detecting and mitigating threats specific to AI systems throughout their life cycle. The examples ISO names publicly are data poisoning and model theft, and it calls out one route for poisoning in particular: data collected while a system is in operation and later reused to retrain it. ISO positions the standard as complementing ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002.

That retraining point is the one most programmes are not set up for. A model that keeps learning from what it sees in production has turned operations into a training pipeline, and a team that guards the original training set but not the feedback loop has left the second door open. European law makes a related demand: Article 15(4) of the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems that continue to learn after deployment to be developed so that biased outputs do not feed future inputs unchecked, and Article 15(5) names data poisoning and model poisoning among the attacks a high-risk system must resist.

What it is not: a certificate

ISO/IEC 27090 is guidance. A certification body audits an organisation against a requirements standard, such as ISO/IEC 27001 for an information security management system or ISO/IEC 42001 for an AI management system. There is no ISO 27090 certificate, and a supplier that claims one is describing something that does not exist.

What an organisation can honestly say is that its security programme took ISO/IEC 27090 into account, and an auditor of a 27001 or 42001 system can ask how AI-specific threats were assessed and treated. The site's AI Assurance Standards page covers how to read each kind of AI assurance claim and what it does and does not prove.

How it got here: the ISO life cycle

The project took a little over four years from approval to publication. The dates below are from ISO's public record of the project's stages.

DateStage
2022-09-15New project approved and registered in the SC 27 work programme
2024-01-23Committee draft (CD) registered
2025-04-16Draft International Standard (DIS) ballot opened
2026-03-12Final Draft International Standard (FDIS) registered for formal approval
2026-08-19FDIS vote closed
2026-10-14Published as edition 1 (stage 60.60)

Commentary written before 14 October 2026 describes the final draft, not the published text, and should be read that way.

How ISO/IEC 27090 relates to the other frameworks

None of the bodies below has published a formal mapping to ISO/IEC 27090 that we have found as of 18 October 2026, and ISO has published none to them. Where this section puts them side by side, the comparison is ours, made from each framework's own public material.

ISO/IEC 42001, the AI management system

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the certifiable standard for running an AI programme: leadership, risk assessment, controls, audit and improvement. It requires AI risks to be assessed and treated; ISO/IEC 27090 is threat-specific security guidance that a 42001 programme can draw on when that treatment turns to attacks on its AI systems. One is the management system, the other is reference material inside it.

ISO/IEC 23894, AI risk management guidance

ISO/IEC 23894:2023 applies general risk management practice to AI across every kind of risk. ISO/IEC 27090 narrows to security threats and compromises. Both are guidance and neither is certifiable, so the practical pairing is 23894 for the risk process and 27090 for the security content that process needs. ISO/IEC 22989, covered on our ISO/IEC 22989 page, supplies the vocabulary all three share.

ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 sets the requirements for an information security management system and ISO/IEC 27002:2022 is the guidance on its controls. ISO says ISO/IEC 27090 complements them. In practice that means AI assets join the existing asset inventory and AI threats join the existing risk assessment, rather than a second AI security programme growing up beside the first. Our ISO 27001 and AI page covers what 27001 already gives an AI programme.

The NIST AI RMF and NIST AI 100-2

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1, January 2023) is the voluntary US framework, and it treats secure and resilient as one of seven characteristics of trustworthy AI. ISO/IEC 27090 is international guidance on that one characteristic. The closer US counterpart is NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, published in March 2025 and free to read. It arranges attacks by machine learning method, life cycle stage and attacker goals, capabilities and knowledge, and it is the most detailed public vocabulary for the attacks ISO names, including poisoning and model theft.

The OWASP LLM and ML Top 10 lists

OWASP's community lists name the same attacks at the application layer. In the Top 10 for LLM Applications, LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning (LLM04 in the 2025 edition) covers poisoning, and model extraction sits under LLM06:2026 Unbounded Consumption (LLM10 in 2025). The OWASP Machine Learning Security Top 10, a 2023 draft, lists ML02 Data Poisoning Attack and ML05 Model Theft. These lists are built for developers and change between editions; ISO/IEC 27090 is a consensus standard on a five-year review cycle. Our AI Security and Risk hub carries every OWASP entry.

MITRE ATLAS

MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on ATT&CK and grounded in case studies of real attacks. It is the natural tool for threat modelling and red-team planning against the threats ISO/IEC 27090 addresses, because it records how attacks have actually been carried out.

EU AI Act Article 15

Article 15 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout their life cycle, and paragraph 5 lists the AI-specific attacks the technical measures should address: data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. It applies from 2 December 2027 for high-risk systems under Annex III and 2 August 2028 for those under Annex I. A presumption of conformity under Article 40 comes from harmonised standards cited in the Official Journal; ISO/IEC 27090 is an international standard, not a harmonised European one, and as of 18 October 2026 we have no record of it being cited. Shared vocabulary between the two is not a legal mapping.

How to put ISO 27090 to work: a 5-step path

These steps are our own practical sequence for a security team that has just heard of the standard. They are not drawn from the standard's text.

  1. Get a licensed copy and read it yourself. The standard's text is sold by ISO, at CHF 204, and by national standards bodies. This page does not summarise it and cannot stand in for it. Decide who in the security team owns the copy and reads it against your own AI systems.
  2. Inventory what an attacker would want. List the AI assets that need protecting: training and fine-tuning data, model weights, system prompts and configuration, retrieval stores, evaluation sets, the retraining pipeline, and every endpoint that returns model output. Put them in the asset register your ISO/IEC 27001 programme already keeps rather than a new one.
  3. Name each threat in a shared vocabulary. Describe threats in terms other people can check: NIST AI 100-2 for the attack and mitigation terms, MITRE ATLAS for techniques observed in real incidents, and the OWASP lists for application-level risks. Record which source each threat came from, so the register can be audited.
  4. Close the retraining loop. Treat data collected in operation as untrusted until it is checked. Record where it came from, gate it before it is reused to train or fine-tune, and keep the ability to roll back to the previous model version if a poisoned update gets through.
  5. Record the treatment where it will be audited. Put the decisions in the risk treatment plan and Statement of Applicability of an ISO/IEC 27001 system, or the AI risk treatment of an ISO/IEC 42001 system, and review them after every model update. Guidance that changes nothing in the audited record changes nothing.

Frequently asked questions about ISO/IEC 27090

Can an organisation be certified to ISO/IEC 27090?

No. ISO/IEC 27090 is guidance, not a requirements standard, so there is nothing for a certification body to certify against. Certification for AI is against ISO/IEC 42001, and for information security against ISO/IEC 27001; either audit can ask how AI-specific threats were handled.

When was ISO/IEC 27090 published?

On 14 October 2026, as edition 1, after its final draft vote closed on 19 August 2026. ISO lists it at 56 pages and CHF 204, from subcommittee ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27, under ICS 35.030.

Does ISO/IEC 27090 replace ISO/IEC 27001 or 27002?

No. ISO describes it as complementing ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002. The management system and its controls stay where they are; ISO/IEC 27090 addresses the threats that are specific to AI systems.

Is ISO/IEC 27090 a harmonised standard under the EU AI Act?

Not as far as we can find. Presumption of conformity under Article 40 of the EU AI Act comes from harmonised standards cited in the Official Journal of the European Union, and as of 18 October 2026 we have no record of ISO/IEC 27090 being cited there. It can still inform how a provider meets the cybersecurity duty in Article 15.

Has ISO published a mapping to NIST, OWASP or MITRE ATLAS?

Not that we have found as of 18 October 2026. The comparisons on this page are our own reading of each framework's public material, and none of them should be treated as an official crosswalk until one of the publishers issues it.

Why does retraining need security attention?

Because data gathered in operation and reused to update a model is a route for poisoning that bypasses whatever checks guarded the original training set. ISO's public description singles out this route, and the EU AI Act's Article 15 treats feedback loops in systems that keep learning as a design duty for high-risk AI.

Can I read ISO/IEC 27090 for free?

No. It is sold by ISO, at CHF 204, and by national standards bodies, and ISO offers a limited preview on its Online Browsing Platform. NIST AI 100-2, MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP lists are free and cover much of the same ground in their own terms.

What independent commentary says

ISO27001security.com, run by IsecT, reviewed the standard at final draft stage in a page last updated 19 August 2026. Its commentary is critical: it argues that the terminology for information risk and security is imprecise, that the focus is on deliberate attacks by capable adversaries rather than accidental failures or insiders, and that the concern is threats to the organisation that owns the AI system rather than misuse of AI against third parties. Those are IsecT's views of the final draft, not ours and not ISO's.

In the research literature, Bunzel (2025), Compliance Made Practical: Translating the EU AI Act into Implementable Security Actions, ties security actions for pretrained and off-the-shelf models to ISO 27090 and to OWASP, which makes it a useful companion for teams working from the EU side.

How this page was written

The facts about the standard on this page, its title, dates, edition, length, price, committee and classification and the description of its scope, come from ISO's public product page as our editor checked it on 18 October 2026. ISO's site terms say ISO content may not be used to prompt or enable AI tools, apart from its Open Data, and the standard itself is copyright. This page was drafted with AI assistance, so it was written only from the editor's verified facts and from independent sources. It does not quote the standard, it does not summarise or paraphrase the standard's clauses, and nothing on it is presented as the standard's wording. For what ISO/IEC 27090 actually says, read a licensed copy.

Primary sources on ISO/IEC 27090

The authoritative pages behind this summary. Where a decision turns on what the standard says, read the standard, not a secondary summary, including this one.

meta_description: ISO/IEC 27090:2026, published 14 October 2026, is guidance on AI-specific security threats such as data poisoning and model theft. What it is and how it relates to ISO 42001, 27001, NIST and the EU AI Act.

security_domains.app: Products built on models inherit their attack surface. Read it beside the OWASP LLM and ML Top 10 lists, which name the same attacks at the application layer.
security_domains.gov: Guidance a risk owner can cite when AI-specific threats go on the register beside ISO/IEC 27001 and 42001. It is guidance, so nothing certifies against it.
security_domains.ops: ISO puts detecting AI-specific attacks in its scope, which makes watching for poisoning and model extraction an operations job as well as an engineering one.
security_domains.arch: Poisoning and model theft are design problems too: isolated training pipelines, limits on what model output exposes, and the ability to roll a model back.
security_domains.data: Training data and data collected in operation are both routes for the poisoning ISO describes, so provenance and checks before data is reused for retraining sit with data protection.
security_domains.tprm: Third-party models, datasets and retraining data bring poisoning risk with them. Ask suppliers how their AI security practice takes ISO/IEC 27090 into account, not whether they are certified to it: no certificate exists.
